A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MiniAppBench benchmark and MiniAppEval framework. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original results for 16 generation models, component ablations, human agreement, double-blind evaluation, and evaluation-trajectory analysis.

after.justification: V3 retains original benchmark experiments and reports additional judge comparisons, sensitivity analyses, dataset statistics, and repeated-generation and repeated-evaluation results.

M1.justification: The generation scaffold, code and DOM inspection, Playwright exploration, three scoring dimensions, and two-stage blind evaluation remain substantively unchanged. The added judge and aggregation comparisons test the existing framework; the revised pass-label boundary is an evaluation-rule change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 500-task benchmark across six domains and retain the 55-query graphical evaluation. V3 newly discloses the direct-user versus augmented-query composition. Its larger expert subset changes sample size, without establishing new task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: V3 adds a systematic comparison of five judge models: GPT-5.2, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, GLM-4.7, Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct, and Gemini-3-Pro-Preview (Tables 10–14). It also compares average-score and median-score criteria against the minimum-score rule. The 16 generation-model comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported pass rule changes from min(score) > 0.8 to min(score) >= 0.8. Ablation and human-agreement subsets change from 183 to 200 items; the human study changes from 549 outputs and 2,196 annotations to 600 outputs and 2,400 annotations. New experiments vary judge, threshold, aggregation rule, and temperature. These revisions do not establish that the unchanged leaderboard and ablation results were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds subset-representativeness analysis, threshold sensitivity and ranking stability, minimum-versus-average/median aggregation comparisons, temperature robustness, and generation/evaluation stability tests (Appendices A.2 and B.3–B.5). These substantially expand validation beyond the retained component ablations, double-blind study, and trajectory-cost analysis.

E5.justification: V3 adds five-run generation and evaluation statistics, including standard deviations, coefficients of variation, per-query consensus, and Fleiss’ kappa. It also reports filtering agreement and threshold-ranking correlations. Human-agreement reporting replaces confusion counts and Cohen’s kappa with judge pass rate, accuracy, and F1, while retaining expert Fleiss’ kappa. The new repeated-run analyses do not establish increased repetitions for the original leaderboard.

E6.justification: The main numerical leaderboard, component-ablation scores, and double-blind results are unchanged, including GPT-5.2’s 45.46% pass rate. V3 adds substantial judge, sensitivity, composition, and stability results; Table 16 reports rank correlations of 0.9765–0.9941. V1’s human-agreement confusion counts and Cohen’s kappa are replaced by pass-rate/accuracy/F1 summaries for a reported 200-item subset, rather than comparable same-setting improvements.

T1.justification: Equation 3 revises the formal positive-label definition from a strict threshold to an inclusive threshold, changing how boundary scores are classified. The dataset tuple and reference-generation mapping remain unchanged; no new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a 500-task benchmark for principle-driven interactive applications, an agentic evaluator, substantial generation difficulty, and strong human alignment. Additional validation supports these existing claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V3 explains the minimum-score rule as requiring every dimension to reach the high-satisfaction band and explains augmentation as counteracting simple, skewed online queries. Appendix C.2 also tempers v1’s claims of eliminating confirmation bias: the findings now suggest reduced contextual bias and are described as consistent with a hypothesis.

D1.justification: V3 newly specifies 77 direct-user and 423 augmented tasks, the filtering models and unanimity rule, the intermediate 1,521-query pool, and judge temperature 1. The abstract’s direct code pointer becomes a homepage pointer. Most implementation details, decoding settings, pseudocode, and prompt instructions are retained; reference-construction prompts remain withheld.

R1.justification: The Cohen (1960) citation and reference disappear with Cohen’s-kappa reporting. The substantive related-work discussion and benchmark positioning remain unchanged. The benchmark-comparison table is relocated, and other reference changes concern formatting or metadata.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence are largely retained. V3 locally rewrites screening and double-blind discussion, adds explanatory subsections, acknowledgements and an impact statement, reorganizes appendix numbering, and updates author-credit text. These are limited editorial changes alongside the scientific additions.

P2.justification: V3 adds extensive structured displays for subset composition and evaluator validation (Tables 7–8 and 10–23), replaces the human-agreement table’s confusion-count/kappa columns, and moves the benchmark comparison into the main text. Conference formatting also changes typography, table placement, and prompt-box presentation. The seven existing figures are retained and reflowed or resized.

improvement.justification: V3 adds useful provenance disclosures and substantial evaluator-validation analyses. However, it replaces auditable confusion counts with summaries for a newly stated 200-item subset without explaining accuracies such as 90.7%, and retains identical ablation values despite the changed sample size. New Table 15 also assigns some ranks inconsistently with its displayed pass rates. These unresolved reporting issues affect the reliability of the added evidence, preventing a confident net-quality judgment.
